x.ASV: Jehovah reigneth; he is clothed with majesty; Jehovah is clothed with strength; he hath girded himself therewith: The world also is established, that it cannot be moved.
x.Darby: Jehovah reigneth, he hath clothed himself with majesty: Jehovah hath clothed himself, he hath girded himself with strength; yea, the world is established, it shall not be moved.
x.KJV: The Lord reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the Lord is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved.
x.YLT: Jehovah hath reigned, Excellency He hath put on, Jehovah put on strength, He girded Himself, Also--established is the world, unmoved.

nt: Verses 1 and 4 of this psalm refer to Yahweh as “he” and verses 2,3, and 5 refer to him as “you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use “you” throughout the psalm, as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is majestic]
גֵּא֪וּת לָ֫בֵ֥שׁ לָבֵ֣שׁ יְ֭הוָה עֹ֣ז הִתְאַזָּ֑ר

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **majesty** and **strength** were actually garments that Yahweh **wears**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he displays his majesty; Yahweh’s strength is obvious for all to see]

The terms **wears** and **girds himself with** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wraps strength all around himself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is obviously powerful]

The expression **is firmly established** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you have firmly established the world]

The expression **be moved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one can ever move it]

x.ASV: Thy throne is established of old: Thou art from everlasting.
x.Darby: Thy throne is established of old; thou art from eternity.
x.KJV: Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting.
x.YLT: Established is Thy throne since then, From the age Thou art.

nt: The expression **is established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You established your throne in ancient times]
Here, **throne** represents royal authority and rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your kingship]

x.ASV: The floods have lifted up, O Jehovah, The floods have lifted up their voice; The floods lift up their waves.
x.Darby: The floods lifted up, O Jehovah, the floods lifted up their voice; the floods lifted up their roaring waves.
x.KJV: The floods have lifted up, O Lord, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves.
x.YLT: Floods have lifted up, O Jehovah, Floods have lifted up their voice, Floods lift up their breakers.

nt: The word translated as **seas** here refers to any kind of moving water; in other contexts it is translated as “rivers” or “floods” (See: “the River” in [Psalms 72:8](../072/008.md)), but “seas” has been chosen here because seas, not rivers, have **pounding waves**.

The psalmist is speaking of **the seas** as if they were living things that could lift their voices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the seas make a roaring noise]

x.ASV: Above the voices of many waters, The mighty breakers of the sea, Jehovah on high is mighty.
x.Darby: Jehovah on high is mightier than the voices of many waters, than the mighty breakers of the sea.
x.KJV: The Lord on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea.
x.YLT: Than the voices of many mighty waters, Breakers of a sea, mighty on high is Jehovah,

nt: מִ⁠קֹּל֨וֹת ׀ מַ֤יִם רַבִּ֗ים אַדִּירִ֣ים מִשְׁבְּרֵי־יָ֑ם אַדִּ֖יר בַּ⁠מָּר֣וֹם יְהוָֽה

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Yahweh on high is mighty** before the comparisons **than the sounds of many waters** and **than the mighty breakers of the sea**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh on high is mightier than the sounds of many waters, than the mighty breakers of the sea]

By **breakers of the sea**, the psalmist means the waves of the sea that crash onto the shore. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [than the mighty waves of the sea crashing on land]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually in a place **on high**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who is greater than everything else]

x.ASV: Thy testimonies are very sure: Holiness becometh thy house, O Jehovah, for evermore.
x.Darby: Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thy house, O Jehovah, for ever.
x.KJV: Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O Lord, for ever.
x.YLT: Thy testimonies have been very stedfast, To Thy house comely is holiness, O Jehovah, for length of days!

nt: Here the psalmist is speaking as if **holiness** were actually a decoration that **adorns** or beautifies the temple. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your house is beautiful because you are holy] or [your holiness is what attracts people to your house]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your house is beautiful because you are holy]

The psalmist is using **length of days** as a common expression of his culture to mean “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for always]
